Under current **Clinical Coverage Policy 3K-2 (CAP/DA)**, the **general eligibility criteria** for CAP/DA services under NC Medicaid are:

## General CAP/DA eligibility

A person must:

- **Be enrolled in NC Medicaid** and not have eligibility restrictions that make them ineligible for the service.
- **Be in Medicaid Direct (fee-for-service)**.
- **Be age 18 or older**.
- **Require an HCBS nursing-facility level of care**, as determined by NC Medicaid.
- **Need long-term care supports** at a level typically provided in an institution, tied to a **documented medical diagnosis and functional care need**.
- Have a **completed CAP assessment** showing a **reasonable indication** that the person will need at least one CAP/DA waiver service within **30 calendar days** of evaluation.
- Be in a **target group documented in the approved waiver application**.
- **Meet applicable Medicaid eligibility criteria** for CAP/DA.
- **Choose the waiver** (freedom of choice), rather than institutional care, when the person meets the level-of-care standard and has a reasonable indication of need for at least one covered waiver service.
- Be **assigned a CAP/DA waiver slot**.
- Have a **signed service plan** authorizing one or more waiver services on a monthly basis, or authorizing short-term installation of equipment/modification/technology to help the person remain in or return to a private residence.
- Be able to have health, safety, and well-being maintained in the **primary private residence or another approved location** using **formal and informal supports**.
- Have paid care needs that can be met **within the average institutional cost** of the CAP/DA waiver.
- Have a **primary physician** who can link and coordinate medical services.
- Have an **emergency back-up and disaster plan** identifying who will provide care if regular caregivers are unavailable.

## Medicaid categories listed in the policy

The policy also lists these Medicaid eligibility categories for CAP/DA:

- **Medicaid to the Aged (MAA)**
- **Medicaid to the Blind (MAB)**
- **Medicaid to the Disabled (MAD)**
- **Health Care for Workers with Disabilities (HCWD)**

## Plain-language summary

In plain terms, CAP/DA is for an **adult Medicaid beneficiary** who is in **Medicaid Direct**, meets **nursing-facility level of care**, can be served safely in the community, has a **documented need for at least one CAP/DA waiver service**, and has an approved **service plan**, available supports, and a **waiver slot**.

## 1) Entrance criteria
Under **Clinical Coverage Policy 8C, Section 3.2.1.1 — "Entrance Criteria"** ([8C, Outpatient Behavioral Health Services Provided by Direct-Enrolled Providers](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/8c-outpatient-behavioral-health-services-provided-direct-enrolled-providers/download?attachment)), outpatient behavioral health services are covered when the beneficiary meets these criteria:

- Has a **current DSM-5 diagnosis** (or subsequent edition).
- Presents **behavioral, psychological, or biological dysfunction and functional impairment** consistent with and associated with the current diagnosis.
- If a **higher level of care is indicated but unavailable**, or the beneficiary is **refusing that service**, outpatient services may be provided until the higher level is available or to support the beneficiary in participating in that higher level of care.
- Is **capable of developing skills** to manage symptoms, make behavioral changes, and respond favorably to therapeutic interventions.
- There is **no evidence that alternative interventions would be more effective**, based on North Carolina community practice standards.

## 2) Continued service criteria
Under **Clinical Coverage Policy 8C, Section 3.2.1.2 — "Continued Service Criteria"** ([8C, Outpatient Behavioral Health Services Provided by Direct-Enrolled Providers](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/8c-outpatient-behavioral-health-services-provided-direct-enrolled-providers/download?attachment)), the beneficiary must meet:

### A. Any **one** of the following:
- The desired outcome or level of functioning has **not been restored, improved, or sustained** over the timeframe in the treatment plan;
- The beneficiary **continues to be at risk for relapse** based on current clinical assessment and history; **or**
- The beneficiary’s functional gains are **tenuous**.

### B. In addition to A, any **one** of the following:
- The beneficiary has **achieved current treatment plan goals**, and **additional goals are indicated** as evidenced by documented symptoms; **or**
- The beneficiary is **making satisfactory progress toward meeting goals** and there is documentation supporting that.

## 3) Discharge criteria
Under **Clinical Coverage Policy 8C, Section 3.2.1.3 — "Discharge Criteria"** ([8C, Outpatient Behavioral Health Services Provided by Direct-Enrolled Providers](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/8c-outpatient-behavioral-health-services-provided-direct-enrolled-providers/download?attachment)), discharge is appropriate when **any one** of the following applies:

- The beneficiary’s **level of functioning has improved** with respect to the goals in the treatment plan;
- The beneficiary or legally responsible person **no longer wishes to receive the services**; or
- The beneficiary, based on presentation and **failure to show improvement despite modifications in the treatment plan**, requires a **more appropriate best practice or evidence-based treatment modality** under North Carolina community practice standards.

## Important related limitation
For context, **Clinical Coverage Policy 8C, Section 4.2.1.1 — "Outpatient Behavioral Health"** says outpatient behavioral health is **not covered** when:

- services are not provided **in person or in accordance with Attachment A**;
- the beneficiary has a **medical, cognitive, intellectual, or developmental issue** that would not benefit from outpatient treatment services; or
- the focus of treatment does **not address the symptoms of the diagnosis**.

Source: **Clinical Coverage Policy 8C, Section 4.2.1.1 — "Outpatient Behavioral Health"** ([8C, Outpatient Behavioral Health Services Provided by Direct-Enrolled Providers](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/8c-outpatient-behavioral-health-services-provided-direct-enrolled-providers/download?attachment)).

## Plain-language summary
A beneficiary can start outpatient behavioral health treatment if they have a current behavioral health diagnosis, impairment related to that diagnosis, and are likely to benefit from outpatient treatment. Services can continue if the person still needs treatment or remains at risk of relapse and is either still progressing or has new documented treatment goals. Discharge is appropriate when goals have been met, the person no longer wants services, or outpatient treatment is no longer the right level or type of care.

per_question.question: Does NC Medicaid cover Personal Care Services for beneficiaries who live in an assisted living facility?

## Which policy applies

For an assisted living facility, the relevant policy is **Clinical Coverage Policy 3L-1, “State Plan Personal Care Services (PCS) Provided in Congregate Settings”**: [State Plan Personal Care Services (PCS) Provided in Congregate Settings](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/media/14986/download?attachment)

I am **not** using **Clinical Coverage Policy 3L, “State Plan Personal Care Services (PCS)”** as the primary source because that policy governs **in-home settings** and includes a section titled **“Personal Care Services in In-Home Settings.”** Its current authoritative version is: [State Plan Personal Care Services (PCS)](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/3l-state-plan-personal-care-services-pcs/download?attachment)

## What 3L-1 says

Under **Clinical Coverage Policy 3L-1, Section 3.2.1 — “Specific criteria covered by Medicaid”**, a beneficiary may qualify for PCS if they:

- have a **medical or mental condition, disability, or cognitive impairment**; and
- demonstrate unmet needs for at least:
  - **three of the five qualifying ADLs with limited hands-on assistance**, or
  - **two ADLs, one of which requires extensive assistance**, or
  - **two ADLs, one of which requires assistance at the full dependence level**; and
- **reside in**:
  - **“a congregate facility licensed by the State of North Carolina as an Adult Care Home (ACH)”**, or
  - certain licensed group homes.

That means the policy expressly contemplates PCS coverage for residents of an **Adult Care Home**, which is the category that generally includes assisted living-type congregate settings.  
Citation: **Clinical Coverage Policy 3L-1, Section 3.2.1 — “Specific criteria covered by Medicaid”**: [State Plan Personal Care Services (PCS) Provided in Congregate Settings](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/media/14986/download?attachment)

## What services are covered

Under **Clinical Coverage Policy 3L-1, Section 3.3 — “Personal Care Services”**, Medicaid covers PCS in congregate settings at minimum once per week, including:

- **hands-on assistance** with qualifying ADLs;
- **set-up, supervision, cueing, prompting, and guiding**, when part of that hands-on assistance;
- assistance with **home management IADLs** directly related to qualifying ADLs and essential to care at the private residence;
- **medication assistance** when directly linked to a documented condition or impairment;
- assistance with **adaptive or assistive devices** tied to qualifying ADLs;
- assistance with **durable medical equipment** tied to qualifying ADLs; and
- **special assistance** requiring a Nurse Aide II and delegated medical monitoring tasks.

Citation: **Clinical Coverage Policy 3L-1, Section 3.3 — “Personal Care Services”**: [State Plan Personal Care Services (PCS) Provided in Congregate Settings](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/media/14986/download?attachment)

## Important limits

Coverage is **not automatic just because someone lives in assisted living**. The beneficiary must also meet the other criteria in **Section 3.2.1**, including that:

- no other third-party payer is responsible for the PCS;
- no family, household member, or informal caregiver is available, willing, and able to provide the authorized services during those times;
- the services are directly linked to a documented condition causing the functional limitations;
- the beneficiary is under the ongoing direct care of a physician; and
- the beneficiary is **medically stable** and **does not require continuous care, monitoring, or supervision by a licensed nurse or other licensed health care professional**.

Citation: **Clinical Coverage Policy 3L-1, Section 3.2.1 — “Specific criteria covered by Medicaid”**: [State Plan Personal Care Services (PCS) Provided in Congregate Settings](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/media/14986/download?attachment)

Also, **Clinical Coverage Policy 3L-1, Section 4.2.1.1 — “Licensed Congregate Facility”** says Medicaid does **not** cover PCS in this setting if the beneficiary:

- is **ventilator dependent**;
- **requires continuous licensed nursing care**;
- has a physician certification that placement is no longer appropriate;
- has health needs that cannot be met in that specific licensed care home; or
- has other medical and functional care needs that cannot be properly met in a licensed care home.

Citation: **Clinical Coverage Policy 3L-1, Section 4.2.1.1 — “Licensed Congregate Facility”**: [State Plan Personal Care Services (PCS) Provided in Congregate Settings](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/media/14986/download?attachment)

## Bottom line

**Yes.** NC Medicaid does cover PCS for some beneficiaries living in an assisted living/adult care home setting, **through Clinical Coverage Policy 3L-1**, if they meet the policy’s functional and medical criteria and the facility setting is one of the licensed congregate settings listed in the policy.

per_question.question: What is the federal statutory authority for NC's CAP/DA waiver, and what does the state need to demonstrate in its waiver application?

To answer what the state must “demonstrate,” I still need the supporting-documentation section that spells out the actual showings behind those assurances.The **federal statutory authority** for North Carolina’s **CAP/DA waiver** is **section 1915(c) of the Social Security Act**, implemented through the federal HCBS waiver regulations in **42 CFR Part 441, Subpart G** and the service definition in **42 CFR 440.180**. The regulations define home- and community-based waiver services as services furnished “under a waiver granted under the provisions of part 441, subpart G.” See **42 CFR 440.180 — "Home and community-based waiver services"** [42 CFR Part 440](https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-42/part-440). The waiver-request rules in **42 CFR 441.301** also expressly refer to the State’s **1915(c) HCBS waiver**. See **42 CFR 441.301 — "Contents of request for a waiver"** [42 CFR Part 441](https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-42/part-441).

## What the state must demonstrate in its waiver application

Under **42 CFR 441.301**, the waiver request must include:

- the **assurances** required by **42 CFR 441.302** and the **supporting documentation** required by **42 CFR 441.303**;
- any requested waivers of Medicaid requirements such as **statewideness**, **comparability**, or certain **income/resource rules for medically needy individuals in the community**, when applicable;
- a statement whether the agency will refuse HCBS when it can reasonably expect the cost to exceed institutional cost; and
- for HCBS specifically, that services will be furnished:
  - under a **written person-centered service plan** approved by the Medicaid agency;
  - only to people who are **not inpatients** of a hospital, nursing facility, or ICF/IID; and
  - only to people whom the agency determines **would require that institutional level of care absent waiver services**.  
  See **42 CFR 441.301 — "Contents of request for a waiver"** [42 CFR Part 441](https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-42/part-441).

## Required assurances the state must make

Under **42 CFR 441.302**, CMS will not grant the waiver unless the state gives satisfactory assurances, including:

- **Health and welfare safeguards**;
- **Financial accountability** for waiver funds;
- **Evaluation and reevaluation** of beneficiaries to determine eligibility and continued need;
- that beneficiaries are **informed of feasible alternatives** and can choose between institutional care and HCBS;
- that the state will apply the proper **post-eligibility treatment of income** where applicable;
- **cost-neutrality / cost estimate assurances** required by the waiver rules.  
See **42 CFR 441.302 — "State assurances"** [42 CFR Part 441](https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-42/part-441).

## Supporting documentation: what the state actually has to show

The most direct answer to “what does the state need to demonstrate?” is in **42 CFR 441.303**, which requires the state to furnish sufficient information supporting those assurances. At a minimum, that includes:

1. **Health and welfare safeguards**  
   A description of the safeguards needed to protect beneficiaries’ health and welfare, including state standards for covered facilities.  
   See **42 CFR 441.303(a)** [42 CFR Part 441](https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-42/part-441).

2. **Financial accountability records**  
   A description of the records and information the state will maintain to support financial accountability.  
   See **42 CFR 441.303(b)** [42 CFR Part 441](https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-42/part-441).

3. **Evaluation and reevaluation process**  
   A description of the state’s plan for evaluating and reevaluating beneficiaries, including:
   - **who** performs evaluations and **how** they are done;
   - the **evaluation form** to be used;
   - if a different form is used than for hospital/NF/ICF-IID placement, an explanation of **how and why it differs** and an assurance that the outcome is **reliable, valid, and fully comparable**;
   - procedures to maintain **written documentation** of evaluations and reevaluations; and
   - procedures to ensure **reevaluations at regular intervals**.  
   See **42 CFR 441.303(c)** [42 CFR Part 441](https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-42/part-441).

4. **Choice of alternatives**  
   A description of how the state will inform eligible beneficiaries of feasible alternatives and allow them to choose either **institutional services or HCBS**.  
   See **42 CFR 441.303(d)** [42 CFR Part 441](https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-42/part-441).

5. **Post-eligibility income/resource treatment**  
   An explanation of how the state will apply post-eligibility treatment of income and resources for beneficiaries receiving HCBS under the special income rule.  
   See **42 CFR 441.303(e)** [42 CFR Part 441](https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-42/part-441).

6. **Cost neutrality / expenditure estimates**  
   Supporting documentation satisfactory to CMS showing **how the state estimated average per capita expenditures** and demonstrating that:
   - the annual average per capita Medicaid cost **with the waiver** does **not exceed**
   - the estimated annual average per capita Medicaid cost **without the waiver**.  
   The regulation states this using the formula **D + D′ ≤ G + G′**.  
   See **42 CFR 441.303(f)(1)** [42 CFR Part 441](https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-42/part-441).

7. **Institutional level of care for diverted persons**  
   For people diverted from institutionalization rather than discharged from an institution, the state must provide a **more detailed description of evaluation and screening procedures** to ensure waiver services are limited to people who would otherwise receive the relevant institutional level of care.  
   See **42 CFR 441.303(f)(5)** [42 CFR Part 441](https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-42/part-441).

8. **Program size / participant cap**  
   The state must indicate the number of **unduplicated beneficiaries** it intends to serve in each program year. That number becomes a limit unless the state later obtains approval for more participants by amendment.  
   See **42 CFR 441.303(f)(6)** [42 CFR Part 441](https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-42/part-441).

## Short plain-language summary

For NC’s **CAP/DA waiver**, the legal authority is **Social Security Act § 1915(c)**. In its waiver application, the state must show CMS that:

- waiver participants would otherwise need an **institutional level of care**;
- services will be delivered under a **person-centered plan**;
- beneficiaries will be protected through **health and welfare safeguards**;
- the state has systems for **financial accountability** and ongoing **reevaluation**;
- people are informed of their **choice** between institutional care and HCBS; and
- the waiver is **cost-neutral**, meaning average Medicaid costs under the waiver will not exceed what Medicaid would have paid without the waiver.

  - dosage and administration; or
  - dosage forms and strengths;

- Use and supervision of volunteers
- Supervision and training plan
- CM orientation plan and annual in-service education plan
- Plan for networking with CCNC or the primary care provider
- Plan for tracking staff skills, abilities, competencies, and knowledge

The agency also must be owned by individuals **not convicted of certain felony offenses**, and must employ or contract with **qualified and trained case managers and supervisors**.

### Training requirements tied to certification
Staff training requirements include:

- Basic training for case managers and supervisors covering:
  - HIV information and prevention techniques
  - CM scope of work
  - Core components of HIV case management
  - Ethical issues in case management
  - Responsibilities/functions of the HIV CM system of care
  - Documentation requirements
- Annual training covering:
  - confidentiality;
  - cultural competency;
  - current trends in HIV disease management;
  - ethics;
  - refresher core components of case management; and
  - treatment of individuals who are HIV positive.

The policy states that **six hours of the twelve-hour annual requirement must be clinically oriented training**.

### Recertification
For recertification, the provider must:

- Submit a **complete and signed Recertification Application** within **60 calendar days of receipt**
- Submit copies of all items from initial certification that have changed
- Submit copies of all HIV CM and supervisor credentials
- Submit annual quality improvement summaries with outcome metrics
- Submit to a **recertification onsite visit**, including review of beneficiary records or other documentation as needed

## Grounds for decertification

A provider may be decertified for any of the following:

- **Failure to provide core service components**
- **Fraudulent billing practices**
- **Owner(s) convicted of a felony charge**
- Failure to develop, submit, and implement a written **plan of correction** for unmet program requirements within **30 calendar days**
- **Falsification of records**
- **Violation of beneficiary confidentiality**
- Employing staff who do not meet Section 6.1 criteria
- Failure of staff to complete mandatory **basic training within 90 days of employment**
- Failure of staff to obtain required **continuing education units**
- Failure to provide supervision sufficient to meet beneficiaries’ needs
- Failure to submit required documentation within required time frames
- Failure to maintain documentation sufficient to support billing
- Failure to implement and enforce a **quality improvement program**
- Failure to timely notify Medicaid/designated contractor of agency changes, resulting in inability to contact the provider
- Failure to comply with applicable **federal and state laws, regulations, reimbursement plan, and Medicaid policies**
- Failure to enroll any beneficiaries within **four months of certification**
- Failure to achieve or maintain certification requirements under Section 6.2  
  **Citation:** **Clinical Coverage Policy 12B, Section 6.2.5 — “Decertification”**: [Human Immunodeficiency Virus (HIV) Case Management](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/12b-human-immunodeficiency-virus-hiv-case-management/download?attachment)

## Bottom line

In plain language, an HIV case management provider must show that it has:

- the **right experience**,
- **qualified case managers and supervisors**,
- required **training and ongoing education**,
- proper **administrative/business infrastructure**,
- a functioning **quality improvement program**,
- required **Medicaid enrollment and accreditation**, and
- ongoing compliance with **documentation, reporting, and oversight** rules.

A provider can be decertified for both **program integrity reasons** (fraud, false records, confidentiality violations, unqualified staff) and **operational noncompliance** (failure to train staff, failure to correct deficiencies, inadequate documentation, failure to maintain certification standards, or failure to serve beneficiaries after certification).
